Context
Following yet another discussion on which Python version we support (#74087) we would like to open a broader discussion on this.
For historical context on how we dealt with 3.6.X versions, we dropped <3.6.2 early on to be able to use features from it #47314. We then moved to 3.7.0 as minimum version when 3.6 reached EOL #71494.
The naming for versions below will be "major.minor.patch".
Related policies are:

from @dagitses that has a draft proposal for versions across multiple dependencies (including Python): #63208

The proposal is to keep minor versions until they reach EOL (5 years after first release right now for CPython).
No details on patch version that we support


NEP 29 that applies to numpy and other sister libraries: https://numpy.org/neps/nep-0029-deprecation_policy.html

Support minor versions for 42 months (3.5 years) after their release.
All patch versions are supported until the minor versions is EOL
This means that numpy right now is 3.8+



Based on this here are two proposals to move forward:
In both cases we will have pip install torch still works just fine. For older versions of Python you will only get the most recent PyTorch version that is available. The difference between the options below is how recent will the version of PyTorch be.
1) Adopt NEP 29

This NEP is very successful for numpy and related libaries (for example jax follows this as well).
It simplifies and reduces cost of maintenance/CI. It is more important to support newer versions quickly than keep supporting old versions for newer releases.
It allows us to use newer Python features much faster.


We will drop support for Python versions much faster than we've been doing up to know (more or less until EOL).

Encountering an issue where the requires_grad field is not being set correctly on forward passes.

During the forward pass, an operation is only recorded in the backward graph if at least one of its input tensors require grad.

We should add support for tensor subclassing.
Today, TorchDynamo will specialize on python classes.  So if you call a function with different tensor subclasses it will compile different graphs.  Currently, there is a filter to just run all tensor subclasses eagerly (for correctness).  Then the question becomes, how do you ahead-of-time turn your graph operating on Tensor subclasses into one using basic tensors ops?
The easier case is __torch_function__, it should be possible to recursively use TorchDynamo to inline the behavior.  If we reimplemented the __torch_function__ dispatching logic in dynamo, it could just treat ops on tensor subclasses as method calls to __torch_function__ and inline them the same way TorchDynamo inlines other method calls.
The harder case is __torch_dispatch__. If the behavior of __torch_dispatch__ is deterministic with respect to what TorchDynamo specializes on, then we can just run it AOT and record the results.  This is what AOT Autograd does.
@ezyang had the idea of a new API that was a static/aot version of the custom __torch_dispatch__ function that operated as graph rewrites.  This would allow tensor subclasses to cooperate with TorchDynamo.  This new API would operate on FX nodes (rather than tensors) to do the transformation.  We may need to add a way to specialize on more than just the type() of the tensor subclas to handle the case that a tensor subclass has extra fields that change the behavior.
If you are interested in experimenting with TorchDynamo + a specific Tensor subclass, you could start by adding your subclass to:
https://github.com/facebookresearch/torchdynamo/blob/00d2af529dc2c98ee201b9503e26bece468d07ea/torchdynamo/utils.py#L79
which allows it to be added to the TorchDynamo generated graph.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Feature: ability to specify the desired indices/rows/cols/diagonal of the inverse so that only the necessary values are calculated.
Most torch.linalg functions are expensive and synchronize with the CPU. As discussed  in #How to speed up linalg operations, this makes them very slow, especially in my case because I need to invert matrices from the forward pass and then backpropagate through the inversions. I have 500,000 samples in my dataset so this now takes ~2.5hrs/epoch instead of ~20min/epoch.
I only need a small fraction of the inverse. The equation I'm using is the following:

where B is a 60x512 matrix, D is 512x512, and lambda comes from the forward pass. The second matrix is zero-padded from 60x512 to 512x512. Therefore, I only need the first 60 rows of the inverse.
Sometimes you might only need certain columns or rows from the inverse. Or the data might have a special structure that could reduce the cost of the inversion. My particular use case would only require providing row and column indices for the inverse.
Alternatives
So far torch.linalg.pinv has worked along with manually defining the left of inverse arguments before using torch.linalg.inv. I have also added code to the initialization to calculate and store the indices needed for the minors so that I can simply use torch.gather to collect the necessary values to compute a partial inverse. However, with limited RAM (both CPU and GPU), a matrix that big is wasteful and often too large to keep in memory.
Additional context
The documentation mentions the GPU/ CPU synchronization for torch.linalg.inv, but I don't understand why that is necessary. I'm sure it is for some reason, but I don't get that part. Maybe a quicker solution would be to eliminate this synchronization and just let it run on the GPU. But as long as this sync slows it down, at least being able to specify what parts of the inverse are needed would be useful to cut down on the expense.

We should generalize the method summon_full_params() to a static method to accommodate being called on a root module that is not an FSDP instance. This avoids having to search for FSDP root instances within the root module and aggregating manually.
For example, right now if we want to compare the parameters of root_module with a fully local version of the model local_model, then we may have to do something like:
params = []
for module in root_module.children():
    context = module.summon_full_params() if isinstance(module, FSDP) else suppress()
    with context:
        params.extend(list(p.detach().clone() for p in module.parameters())
# Now we can correctly call `zip(params, local_model.parameters())`

We should place this kind of logic behind our API. The generalization should be similar to the above only using yield instead of explicitly constructing a list and not detach().clone()-ing since the memory should be safe to access while inside the context.

We currently handle aliasing of objects that (could) have side effects here.  But there are no guards checking that the aliasing relationships stay the same in subsequent calls.  This could lead to incorrect behavior in an example like this:
def foo(left, right, x):
  left.append(x+1)
  right.append(x-1)
  return left, right

a, b, c = [], []. []
with torchdynamo.optimize(...):
   foo(a, b)  # this works fine

torchdynamo.reset()
with torchdynamo.optimize(...):
   foo(c, c)  # this works fine too

a, b, c = [], []. []
torchdynamo.reset()
with torchdynamo.optimize(...):
   foo(a, b)  # correct
   foo(c, c)  # aliasing relationship changed!  wrong behavior!

a, b, c = [], []. []
torchdynamo.reset()
with torchdynamo.optimize(...):
   foo(c, c)  # correct
   foo(a, b)  # aliasing relationship changed! wrong behaivor!

We should add a set of guards that check for this case and trigger a recompile.  We likely need some sort of hash table to do these checks quickly.  Adding similar protection for Tensor aliasing would likely also be useful for compiler backends, as it will allow them to generate code that relies on input aliasing being unchanged.

Inline the forward() in eval() mode
Break the graph in train() mode

Use TorchDynamo to trace the forwards
Use TorchDynamo to trace the backwards (need example inputs here)
If they both trace, construct a new autograd.Function to put in the generated FX graph.
Need some glue to connect this with AOT Autograd if there are side-effects,etc that dynamo needs to handle with Python code.

Today, everything after an exception won't be captured by TorchDynamo:
try:
   x = x + 1  # should be captured fine
   assert False
except:
   x = x + 2  # won't be captured
   return x

To add support for this there are two main cases:

Both the raise and the except are in the same capture context.  In this case TorchDynamo can remove the raise and combine the above example into a single graph.  Logically the raise becomes a jump.
The raise/except is in a different capture contexts.  In this case we need to actually throw the exception.  To handle this case we need extend our resume_execution codegen to put the exception handler in a new python function/frame.  This allows dynamo to capture the body of the except as if it were defined in a function.  I started implementing this, but never finished it.

Handling the first case seems more useful, but eventually we need to handle both.

Torch.package  is a handy tool to serialize and deserialize python code. It works as you expect a packager to but with the added benefit of also saving the actual code itself when desired. It was primarily designed with the intention of being the delivery mechanism for torch::deploy which is a runtime for getting pytorch models to run on multiple threads in eager mode. There's a great whitepaper about torch.package and torch::deploy here.
Motivation: So for all cases it ends up that Python isn't actually BC (Backwards compatible). We want there to be a way to record the python version of a package, so the user can check if they are on a different version of python to detect these bugs.
We should add which version of python is used to the torch.package metadata. We can likely just store this in a metadata file in the .data folder created by torch.package.
In order to do this,

In torch/package/package_exporter when we write the final zip file, create a new file in the .data folder and stick the python version in there.
Create a function in the package importer in order to inspect which python version a torch.package came from. In order to have BC, we should say that the package is older than this feature was added if it doesn't exist.
Create a small test in test/package/test_misc.py that creates a package and makes sure it contains the current python version. Some examples of how we create packages for unit tests can be found in test/package/test_misc.py, test/package/test_dependency_api.py, and pretty much most of the unit tests under test/package. Furthermore, we have a tutorial as well.
Create another test for BC purposes. Create a small package and save it into the repo. Then another test in test/package/test_misc.py just checks that the package contains the correct python version which it was made from.

To run your tests just run python test/package/test_misc.py (for OSS)

🐛 Describe the bug
Problem: torch.nn.Module.__init__ does not call super().__init__()
Consequence: Mixin-type classes (example and example) must be put before any nn.Module in __mro__.
This makes for an amazing foot-gun when composing models using mixins that are not not only used for nn.Modules, and thus cannot specify it as its parent.
Reproduction:
from torch import nn

class MyMixin:
    def __init__(self, *a, **kw):
        super().__init__(*a, **kw)
        print("MyMixin.__init__")

class MyModuleWithMixinBefore(MyMixin, nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        print("MyModuleWithMixinBefore.__init__")

class MyModuleWithMixinAfter(nn.Module, MyMixin):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        print("MyModuleWithMixinAfter.__init__")

module1 = MyModuleWithMixinBefore()
print(*(f" - {i.__module__}.{i.__name__}" for i in MyModuleWithMixinBefore.__mro__), sep="\n")

print()

module2 = MyModuleWithMixinAfter()
print(*(f" - {i.__module__}.{i.__name__}" for i in MyModuleWithMixinAfter.__mro__), sep="\n")
Output:
MyMixin.__init__
MyModuleWithMixinBefore.__init__
 - __main__.MyModuleWithMixinBefore
 - __main__.MyMixin
 - torch.nn.modules.module.Module
 - builtins.object

MyModuleWithMixinAfter.__init__
 - __main__.MyModuleWithMixinAfter
 - torch.nn.modules.module.Module
 - __main__.MyMixin
 - builtins.object

Of note is how MyMixin.__init__ is not printed for MyModuleWithMixinAfter.

Add super().__init__() to torch.nn.Module.__init__ after all the class members have been set.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Most of our creation ops come in pairs:

full / full_like
zeros / zeros_like
rand / rand_like
...

The *_like variant takes another tensor as reference and copies its shape and the core attributes. The attributes can be overwritten by keyword argument however, e.g.
>>> a = torch.zeros(1, 2, 3, dtype=torch.float)
>>> b = torch.zeros_like(a, dtype=torch.int)
>>> assert a.shape == b.shape
>>> assert b.dtype == torch.int
One creation op that has no _like variant is torch.tensor.
I propose to add it and to let it behave just like the other variants with the only difference that we don't take the shape from the reference. Thus, tensor_like would only copy the attributes.
I often find myself doing torch.tensor(..., dtype=other.dtype, device=other.dtype) when I need specific values, but otherwise want to align it with a reference. It would be more concise and less error-prone to do torch.tensor_like(other, ...). Plus it conveys the intent better.
Alternatives
I also often see something like
torch.tensor(...).to(other)
which potentially adds an unnecessary copy.

Now we have dist.gather support on NCCL, but ShardedTensor.gather couldn't use it for some reasons:

We can use gather_object for metadatas, but we couldn't simply use gather for the local shard tensors, mainly because local_shards() is a list of tensor, but input of gather is a single tensor not a list of tensor, so gather won't work here
We can try using torch.cat locally on each rank to form a single tensor before the gather collective, but we need to split them afterwards as they might not be adjacent to each other (local shards on this rank might contain two tensors that's far away in the global position logically). 🐛 Describe the bug
When implementing a custom Lazy Tensor Core backend with custom autogen, I get many many warnings similar to
[W OperatorEntry.cpp:133] Warning: Overriding a previously registered kernel for the same operator and the same dispatch key
  operator: aten::_log_softmax(Tensor self, int dim, bool half_to_float) -> (Tensor)
    registered at aten/src/ATen/RegisterSchema.cpp:6
  dispatch key: Lazy
  previous kernel: registered at aten/src/ATen/RegisterCPU.cpp:21233
       new kernel: registered at csrc/backend/RegisterLazy.cpp:2070 (function registerKernel)

Looking at it more closely, the previous kernel registration occurs at aten/src/ATen/RegisterCPU.cpp:21233 where I see
TORCH_LIBRARY_IMPL(aten, CPU, m) {
And csrc/backend/RegisterLazy.cpp:2070 has
TORCH_LIBRARY_IMPL(aten, Lazy, m) {
Which clearly shows that the dispatch keys are different. So, the Overriding a previously registered kernel for the same operator and the same dispatch key message is either misleading or there is a bug in the logic that checks for previous registrations.
I suspect that its the former. My suspicion is that the definitions for those operators that I'm seeing warnings for are clashing with definitions of these operators in the TorchScript backend. i.e. they are being registered by the TS backend first and then being reregistered by my custom backend. In which case, for Lazy Tensor Core, there needs to be some mechanism put into place so that the operator kernels only get registered when the backend gets initialized instead of when the dynamic library containing the symbols is loaded (which is what's currently happening).

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
FSDP flatten parameters and shard these flatten parameters among ranks.  After that, these sharded flatten parameters are passed to optimizers. Optimizers will optimize for these sharded flatten parameters locally in the training loop.
When saving original unflatten parameters' states in optimizer, we need APIs to help all_gather the sharded flatten parameters, and then unflatten them back to original ones. Also, for non-tensor states or local states, FSDP needs to make sure they are saved properly as well for the optimizers.
before calling optimizer.load_state_dict() for FSDP model, FSDP needs APIs to load these saved original unflatten parameters' states, flatten them, shard them and then pass the sharded states to optimizer.load_state_dict().
The implementation will be similar to 'gather_full_optim_state_dict()' and 'get_shard_from_optim_state_dict()' in FairScale FSDP. In default, for parameters' states, it can output states with "indexes" as keys. But based on users' needs, we may provide one more option to output states with  "parameter names" as keys.
An example to save optimizer states:
fsdp_model = fsdp(model, old_process_group)
optimizer = torch.adam(fsdp_model.parameters())
..... (training loop)
full_optim_state_dict = fsdp_model.gather_full_optim_state_dict(optimizer)
file = torch.save(full_optim_state_dict)
An example to load optimizer states with new process group and new world_size:
fsdp_model = fsdp(model, new_process_group)
optimizer = torch.adam(fsdp_model.parameters())
full_optim_state_dict = torch.load(file)
optimizer.load_state_dict(fsdp_model.get_shard_from_optim_state_dict(full_optim_state_dict))
# training loop
.....

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Motivation
I've been writing up a small document on NumPy compatibility over at #71688 and one of the things which stood out is that there is no current mechanism to provide optional details without directing the reader to an issue or pull request comment. In that PR, the optional details would be this block describing the code path taken upon execution of the example; which was adapted from this issue comment.
Pitch
We need a documentation structure which is:

Optional --> The remaining text should not rely on the contexts of this portion of the document
Unobtrusive --> The documentation should be easy to avoid and must not break the flow of the current text

Solution
The solution is an additional information / details dropdown element which can be implemented easily with sphinx-panels (found here). For a completely contrived example:
.. dropdown:: Click on me to see my content!

    I'm the content which can be anything:

    .. link-button:: https://example.com
        :text: Like a Button
        :classes: btn-primary
Will render to the pleasantly optional:

Additionally, as the PyTorch documentation already loads Bootstrap classes, we don't add anything heavy in terms of the CSS / JS dependencies.
Alternatives
The current mechanisms for adding context to the main document are:

Admonitions (note, warning, etc.)
Footnotes

Neither of these are suitable for the kind of detail provided by a dropdown. Admonitions break the flow of the text and are always used to highlight text, while footnotes can be jarring to work with for long documents, and the diminished font-size make it impractical for longer discussions.
Additional context
See #73836 for an implementation.
Pinging @rgommers for comments.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Currently, FSDP does not recursively wrap submodules by default, which can result in some usability issues as all users will have to figure out a wrapping policy for their use case or manually annotate some models with wrap().
We could run some experiments on key workloads and come up with a general policy, perhaps based on # of parameters to wrap, that appropriately trades off performance with memory saving goals and is ideal for a wide variety of workloads, and then recursively wrap FSDP with this policy by default.
This approach is similar to DDP bucketing where default size of 25 mb works well for many applications via experimentation.
One issue is backwards compatibility, i.e. using recursive wrap with policy by default might break enable_wrap + wrap() API approach.
